title: Volkswagen
wiki_lead:
Volkswagen (German pronunciation: [ˈfɔlksˌvaːɡŋ̍] ), commonly abbreviated to VW, is a German automobile brand based in Wolfsburg, Lower Saxony, Germany. Established in 1937 by the German Labour Front, it was revived after World War II by British Army officer Ivan Hirst and grew into a global brand. As of 2025, the company had a market capitalization of approximately US$58.9 billion.
The name Volkswagen derives from the German words Volk ('people') and Wagen ('wagon'), meaning 'people's car', or more directly 'folk's wain (wagon)'.

Volkswagen (German pronunciation: [ˈfɔlksˌvaːɡŋ̍] ), commonly abbreviated to VW, is a German automobile brand based in Wolfsburg, Lower Saxony, Germany. Established in 1937 by the German Labour Front, it was revived after World War II by British Army officer Ivan Hirst and grew into a global brand. As of 2025, the company had a market capitalization of approximately US$58.9 billion.
The name Volkswagen derives from the German words Volk ('people') and Wagen ('wagon'), meaning 'people's car', or more directly 'folk's wain (wagon)'.


History


1932–1938: People's Car project
Volkswagen was established in 1937 by the Nazi Party's German Labour Front (Deutsche Arbeitsfront) as part of the Strength Through Joy (Kraft durch Freude, abbreviated to KdF) program in Berlin. In the early 1930s, cars were a luxury; most Germans could afford nothing more elaborate than a motorcycle, and only one out of 50 Germans owned a car. Seeking a potential new market, some car makers began independent "people's car" projects – the Mercedes 170H, BMW 3/15, Adler AutoBahn, Steyr 55 and Hanomag 1.3 L (79 in3), among others.
The growing trend was not new; Béla Barényi, a pioneering automotive engineer, is credited as already having conceived the basic design during the mid-1920s. Josef Ganz developed the Standard Superior (going as far as to advertise it as the "German Volkswagen"). In Germany, Hanomag mass-produced the 2/10 PS Kommissbrot, a small, cheap rear-engined car, from 1925 to 1928. Also, in Czechoslovakia, the Hans Ledwinka-designed Tatra T77, a very popular car amongst the German elite, was becoming smaller and more affordable at each revision. Ferdinand Porsche, a well-known designer for high-end vehicles and race cars, had been trying for years to get a manufacturer interested in a small car suitable for a family. He built a car known as the Volksauto from the ground up in 1933, using many popular ideas and several of his own, putting together a car with an air-cooled rear engine, torsion bar suspension, and a "beetle" shape, the front bonnet rounded for better aerodynamics (necessary as it had a small engine).

In 1934, with many of the aforementioned projects still in development or early stages of production, Adolf Hitler became involved, ordering the production of a basic vehicle capable of transporting two adults and three children at 100 km/h (62 mph). He wanted a car every German family would be able to afford. The "People's Car" would be available through a savings plan at 990 ℛ︁ℳ︁, equivalent to €4,688 in 2021 – about the price of a small motorcycle (the average income being around 32 ℛ︁ℳ︁ a week, equivalent to €152 in 2021).
It soon became apparent that private industry could not turn out a car for only 990 ℛ︁ℳ︁. Thus, Hitler chose to sponsor an all-new, state-owned factory using Ferdinand Porsche's design (with some of Hitler's design suggestions, including an air-cooled engine so nothing could freeze). The intention was that German families could buy the car through a savings scheme ("Fünf Mark die Woche musst du sparen, willst du im eigenen Wagen fahren", transl. "You need to set aside five marks a week, if you want to drive in your own car"), which around 336,000 people eventually paid into. However, the project was not commercially viable, and only government support was able to keep it afloat. Due to the outbreak of World War II in 1939, none of the participants in the savings scheme ever received a car. In 1950, a lawsuit was issued that, after 12 years of trial, ultimately provided a credit of 12% off the list price of a new VW base model or roughly 20% of the value originally paid into the saving scheme.
Prototypes of the car called the KdF-Wagen (from the German term Kraft durch Freude, meaning 'strength through joy') first appeared in 1938. The first cars had been produced in Stuttgart. grok_lead: Volkswagen AG is a German multinational conglomerate that manufactures automobiles, commercial vehicles, and related components, headquartered in Wolfsburg, Lower Saxony, with approximately 672,000 employees worldwide. Founded on May 28, 1937, by the Nazi-controlled German Labour Front as the Gesellschaft zur Vorbereitung des Deutschen Volkswagens mbH, the company was tasked with producing the KdF-Wagenâan affordable "people's car" conceived by Adolf Hitler and designed by Ferdinand Porsche âto motorize the German populace under the regime's propaganda initiative. During World War II, the factory shifted to military production and relied on forced labor from concentration camps, producing few civilian vehicles before Allied bombing halted operations. Postwar, under British Army oversight led by Major Ivan Hirst, Volkswagen restarted civilian production in 1945, with the refined KdF-Wagen evolving into the iconic Beetle (Type 1), which became a global bestseller with over 21 million units sold by 1974 due to its simple, reliable rear-engine design and low cost. The company's expansion in the 1960s and 1970s included diversification into new models like the Golf hatchback, introduced in 1974 as the Beetle's successor, which has sold more than 35 million units and solidified Volkswagen's reputation for practical, front-wheel-drive engineering. Today, as the Volkswagen Group, it encompasses 12 brandsâincluding Audi, Porsche, and Bentley. In July 2026, amid declining sales (second-quarter global deliveries fell 8.6% to just under 2.1 million vehicles, with China down more than one-third), the company announced plans to slash its model range by up to half and reduce annual production capacity to about 9 million vehicles as part of a broader restructuring. It generates sales revenue exceeding â¬300 billion, positioning it among the world's largest automakers by volume and revenue. Volkswagen's history is marked by significant controversies, notably the 2015 Dieselgate scandal, where the company admitted to equipping about 11 million diesel vehicles with software "defeat devices" that detected testing conditions and reduced emissions only during lab evaluations, allowing real-world nitrogen oxide outputs up to 40 times legal limits in the United States. This systematic deception, driven by internal pressures to meet stringent regulations while preserving diesel performance, led to over $30 billion in global fines, recalls, and settlements, alongside criminal convictions of executives and a reevaluation of the firm's corporate governance. Despite these setbacks, Volkswagen has pursued electrification, investing heavily in battery-electric vehicles under its ID. series to address environmental critiques rooted in its diesel legacy.
